beach_verdict: Pick ISLA BARU, and stay on the quiet south/southwest side rather than on the Playa Blanca day-tripper strip. BarU is the only one of the five options that gives a group of five a real four-night base instead of a logistics exercise. It is joined to the mainland by the Barbacoas bridge, so you reach it in about an hour by road and you can leave whenever you like; every other candidate locks you into fixed boat windows. That matters specifically in early March: the December-to-May trade winds blow hard over this coast, mornings are calm and afternoons get choppy, so the Rosario and San Bernardo crossings (45-60 min and 2h+ of open water respectively, with a mandatory 3-4pm return) are the ones you least want to be committed to four days running. From Baru you still get the good water, because the Rosario reefs are a 20-40 minute private-boat hop and you go in the morning when the sea is flat. Playa Blanca itself is genuinely overrun between roughly 11am and 4pm by day boats and vendors, but if you sleep on the island it empties at dusk and dawn and is yours. Barú also owns the four best non-beach things to do down there: the bioluminescent plankton lagoon at Manzanillo (a night activity, so only stayers get it), the Aviario Nacional, the mangrove channels for kayaking, and Cholón. Runner-up, and the honest alternative if water clarity is the single thing you care about: ISLA GRANDE in the Rosarios, but take two nights there, not four, and expect rustic-not-designed hotels, rocky entries and one boat a day. Rejected: Tierra Bomba (15 min away and great for a day, but the water is brackish and mediocre and it is not a four-night place), Santa Marta/Tayrona/Palomino (a flight or a 4-5h drive, and most Tayrona beaches are closed to swimming for current - it breaks the no-moving rule), Isla Mucura/San Bernardo (beautiful, arguably the best water of all, but 2h+ of open sea each way in the windiest month with almost no exit options). BUDGET REALITY: the genuinely beautiful design hotels on Barú (Las Islas, Sofitel Barú Calablanca) sit at USD 430-460 a night, more than double the cap. Inside USD 200 you get pleasant, low-key, eco-ish places, not Mr & Mrs Smith material. The strongest move for five people is an Airbnb villa with a private pool split five ways - on Barú that is where the design and the value both are.

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias
stops.area_note: Stay inside the walls. El Centro is the postcard half (cathedral, Plaza Santo Domingo, the best restaurants) and is the most expensive; San Diego is the same walled city but quieter, more residential and slightly cheaper - for a group of five with taste, San Diego is the sweet spot. Getsemaní is 10 minutes' walk outside the Clock Tower gate, scruffier, covered in murals, and where the bars, Celele, Alquímico and Café Havana are; rooms there run roughly 20-30 percent under Centro for the same quality. HONEST WARNING ON BUDGET: early March is peak high season in Cartagena (the high-season block runs mid-January through March and prices run roughly 1.5-2x low season). USD 200 a double is workable but it is not generous - it buys you the good second tier (Kartaxa, Casa del Coliseo, Casa Pizarro, Townhouse), not the famous ones. The trophy hotels are far out of reach: Casa San Agustín is around USD 673 a night, Casa Pestagua around USD 709, Sofitel Legend Santa Clara around USD 593, the new Four Seasons around USD 690. Book 2-3 months out; the small boutiques inside the walls sell out for March.

activities.name: Walled-city orientation walk and sunset on the muralla
activities.what: Land, drop bags, then walk Centro to San Diego to Las Bóvedas and up onto the sea wall for sunset. Three ways to do the sunset drink: Café del Mar, literally built on top of the ramparts, iconic and packed - reserve or arrive by 4:30pm, premium prices; Baluarte de Santo Domingo next door, much less crowded and noticeably cheaper; or Townhouse rooftop in San Diego, two wading pools and a sunset DJ, pool access around 50,000 COP. If you want the 360-degree view over old city, bay and skyline rather than just the sea, the Movich rooftop one block off Plaza Bolívar beats all of them - it is open to the public but closes for private events, so call ahead.
activities.when: Day 1, 16:00 onwards (sunset roughly 18:10 in early March)

activities.name: First dinner: La Cevichería
activities.what: The Bourdain ceviche place on Calle Stuart by Plaza San Diego. Small, courtyard-ish, no reservations historically so go at 6:30pm or expect to queue. Mains $13-23. If the queue is brutal, El Boliche Cebichería a few streets away is the locals' better-value answer at $12-21.

activities.name: Bazurto market food tour
activities.what: Not the tourist version of Cartagena: the real wholesale market east of the centre, with a guide, eating your way through fruit stalls, fried-food stands, butchers and a sit-down lunch. Cartagena Connections and Juan Ballena both run it, typically a 10:30am start with local bus transport, fruit tasting and lunch included. Go with an operator, not alone.

activities.name: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, late afternoon
activities.what: The big hilltop fortress with the tunnel network. Go at 16:00-17:30, not midday - there is no shade and March sun is punishing. Roughly an hour and a half including the tunnels and the view back over the old city.

activities.name: Celele, then champeta at Bazurto Social Club
activities.what: Celele in Getsemaní is the reason food people fly here - No.5 in Latin America's 50 Best 2025, No.48 in the World's 50 Best, Caribbean-Colombian cooking from the Caribe Project research. Mains $16-23, tasting menu around $78. Reservations are effectively mandatory: they lock the door after check-in, require a card and a minimum spend, and you need a week ahead on weekdays and a couple of weeks for a weekend. Afterwards walk five minutes to Bazurto Social Club on Avenida del Centenario for live champeta and picó sound-system culture - the Palenque/Afro-Caribbean side of this city that the walled city hides.

activities.name: Getsemaní street-art and culture walk
activities.what: Two to three hours through the murals, Calle de la Sierpe, Plaza de la Trinidad and the Callejón Angosto umbrellas, with the gentrification and Afro-Caribbean history that goes with them. The shared graffiti walk is about $15-40; the private version with a snack runs nearer $40-60. Do it in the morning before the heat.

activities.name: Volcán del Totumo mud volcano (optional, judge it honestly)
activities.what: A 15-metre mud cone about an hour north where you climb in and float in warm grey clay, then rinse in the lagoon. Group half-day tours $35-45pp, small-group or private $50-65, or $5-6 at the gate if you drive yourself. Worth knowing: it is kitschy, crowded, and the 'massage' and 'photo help' and 'wash' each come with a $2 tip expectation that stacks up. Skip it if your group would rather have a proper Caribbean cooking class instead (roughly $70-90pp) - both fill the same morning slot.

activities.name: Sunset sail on the bay, then chiva or Alquímico
activities.what: A shared sunset catamaran across Cartagena bay, roughly 90 minutes to two hours, $25-50pp, usually with an open bar of rum drinks; Sibarita Express is the commonly recommended one. Private charters for the whole group run $500-750 for the evening. Then choose your night: the chiva rumbera painted party bus with a brass band and an aguardiente open bar (about $25-40pp, 3 hours, deliberately ridiculous), or the grown-up version - Alquímico on Calle del Colegio, three floors, herb-infused bottles glowing on two-storey shelves, a World's 50 Best Bars regular - followed by salsa at Café Havana in Getsemaní.

food.name: Celele
food.what: Colombian Caribbean, Latin America's 50 Best No.5, Getsemaní. Mains $16-23, tasting around $78. Book 1-2 weeks ahead, card required.

food.name: Carmen
food.what: Caribbean ingredients, European technique, El Centro. Mains $18-27, tasting $68-83. The other fine-dining anchor alongside Celele.

food.name: Marea by Rausch
food.what: Seafood and risotto on the Getsemaní waterfront by the Rausch brothers. $22-34 per person. The best of the smart-but-not-tasting-menu tier.

food.name: La Cevichería
food.what: The Bourdain ceviche house, Calle Stuart near Plaza San Diego, El Centro. $13-23. Go early, it queues.

food.name: La Cocina de Pepina
food.what: Proper costeño home cooking in Getsemaní - arroz de lisa, posta cartagenera. $9-15. The cheap meal you will actually talk about.

stops.weather_note: Early March is the dry season and about as good as this coast gets: lows around 24-25C, highs 30-32C, sea temperature 28-29C, roughly 11.6 hours of sun and very little rain. The catch is wind. December through May the trade winds blow steadily over the Caribbean coast and March sits inside that window - it keeps the city bearable and it keeps the mosquitoes down, but it also churns the sea. Mornings are calm; the water builds through the afternoon. That is why every boat thing in this plan is scheduled before noon. March is also firmly high season (the block runs mid-January to March, at roughly 1.5-2x low-season rates), so prices are at their annual peak and the good restaurants and small hotels need booking weeks out.

stops.name: Isla Barú (Playa Blanca / south Barú)
stops.area_note: Barú is technically a peninsula, cut off by the Canal del Dique and reconnected by road in 2014, which is the whole point: you drive there in about an hour and you are not hostage to a boat schedule. Three distinct zones. (1) The Playa Blanca strip in the north - the famous white sand, and also the problem: day boats and vans dump crowds and vendors on it from roughly 11am to 4pm. Stay at the quiet end of it (Thani Ecobeach) and it empties completely at dusk. (2) The Cholón-facing west side - calmer water, the party-boat lagoon a short hop away, where Aura sits. (3) The south and southwest end past the Aviario - the best beaches, the fewest people, and where Sabai, Casa Córdoba, Las Islas and Isla del Encanto are. For a design-conscious group that wants a scene without a party hostel, the south end is right, with one big private-boat day out to the Rosarios and Cholón from there. BUDGET REALITY: the postcard hotels here are out of range - Las Islas is $460+ a night ($230pp) and Sofitel Barú Calablanca $430+ ($215pp). Inside $200 you get good, low-key, eco-leaning places. An Airbnb villa with a private pool split five ways is the better-looking and better-value play on this island.

activities.name: Transfer to Barú, then Playa Blanca after the day boats leave
activities.what: Private van from the walled city over the Barbacoas bridge, about 1h-1h15 door to door, roughly 350,000-450,000 COP (USD 85-110) for a van of five - have the hotel arrange it. Check in, then walk out onto Playa Blanca at about 16:30 once the day boats and vans have gone. This is the version of that beach worth seeing: same white sand, no vendors, no crowd, low light.

activities.name: Bioluminescent plankton night swim
activities.what: Small boat out into the dark mangrove lagoon near Manzanillo del Mar / Portonaito, where the dinoflagellates light up blue when you move the water. This is the single best argument for sleeping on Barú rather than day-tripping it, because it only runs at night. Standalone from a Barú hotel, roughly $25-35pp; as a packaged evening excursion from Cartagena, $50-70pp. Go on the darkest night you can - it is washed out by a bright moon, so check the moon phase for your dates before you book.

activities.name: Private boat charter: Rosario Islands, snorkelling and Cholón
activities.what: The big day, and the reason Barú works. Charter your own speedboat rather than joining a day tour: a 28ft (10-12 pax) runs from 1,800,000 COP, about USD 450, and a 29ft from about USD 475, captain and fuel included, cooler and sound system on board. Split five ways that is USD 90-95 each - far better than the $93-125pp beach-club day passes and you control the route. Standard run: leave around 08:30 while the sea is flat, snorkel the Rosario reefs (10-15m visibility, protected marine park), lunch at one of the island clubs, then Cholón in the afternoon - the anchored-boat lagoon where everyone rafts up, sound systems competing, floating bars selling ceviche and mojitos. Loud, messy, very Colombian, and much better on a boat you control. Budget an extra USD 7.50pp national park fee and USD 2pp maritime insurance, cash only.
activities.when: Day 5 - and do it on your first clear morning, not the afternoon

activities.name: Aviario Nacional de Colombia
activities.what: On Barú itself, so no boat: 21 exhibits across three reconstructed ecosystems, 170-odd species, two daily flight demonstrations with a handler. Genuinely well done and the best rainy-hour or windy-morning fallback on the island. Foreign adult admission is 90,000 COP (about USD 22) as of September 2026, students 65,000 COP.

activities.name: Kayak the mangrove channels, then nothing
activities.what: The lagoon side of Barú is threaded with mangrove channels you can paddle through in flat water even when the sea outside is blown out - which in March it often is by mid-afternoon. Several hotels lend the kit free: Thani Ecobeach includes a double kayak and a paddleboard at no charge. Then deliberately do nothing for the rest of the day. On a four-night beach stop, one empty day is the point.
activities.duration: 2 hours plus the rest of the day

activities.name: Morning snorkel or a beach-club day pass
activities.what: Two ways to close it out. Either a half-day snorkel run to the Rosario coral gardens, roughly $40-70pp through your hotel - again, morning, when the water is clearest and calmest. Or take a day pass at one of the designed beach clubs and spend the day horizontal: on Barú, Nena Beach Club, Sabai Beach Club, Mambo or Sunset Beach Club; none charge a dock fee if you arrive by land. In the Rosarios, mid-range passes run $93-125pp including boat and lunch (Capri, Pa'ue, Mangata), which is why the private charter on day 5 is the better spend.

activities.name: Last sunset, west-facing
activities.what: Barú faces west, so unlike Cartagena you get the sun dropping into open water straight off your own beach. No booking, no boat, no price. Then back to Cartagena on day 8 by road, roughly an hour, and out.

food.name: Your hotel restaurant
food.what: Be realistic: Barú is not a restaurant destination. Most nights you eat where you sleep. Budget $15-30pp at Thani or Aura, more at Sabai. Thani's food is good but reviewers flag small portions for the price.

food.name: Playa Manglares Isla Barú
food.what: The property on the island with an actual food reputation - worth booking a table even if you are staying elsewhere. Roughly $25-40 per person.

food.name: Sabai Beach restaurant
food.what: Open to non-guests as well as guests, on the private beach at the southwest tip. The nicest setting for a long lunch on the island. $30-50 per person.

food.name: Nena Beach Club, Playa Blanca
food.what: Beach-club lunch on the famous sand - loungers, fried fish and coconut rice, cocktails. Usually structured as a day pass or a minimum spend, roughly $30-50 per person.

food.name: Cholón floating vendors
food.what: Not a restaurant: boats that pull alongside yours in the lagoon selling ceviche, oysters and cocktails. Cash, and agree the price before anything is handed over. $10-20 per person.

stops.weather_note: Same dry-season numbers as Cartagena - 30-32C, sea at 28-29C, almost no rain - but on Barú the wind is not a footnote, it is the thing that shapes your days. December to May the trade winds blow hard over this stretch, and the practical effect is that mornings are glassy and afternoons get choppy, with afternoon boat crossings described by local guides as genuinely challenging. Three consequences: book every boat activity for the morning; expect Playa Blanca's water to go from turquoise to stirred-up and greenish on the windiest afternoons, sometimes with seaweed; and be aware the wind masks the sun, so people burn badly here without noticing. The upside is real too - it is the driest, clearest, least-mosquito time of year, and 11-plus hours of sun a day.

getting_around: IN CARTAGENA: the walled city and Getsemaní are small and walkable - ten to fifteen minutes end to end, and about ten minutes between the two through the Clock Tower gate. Taxis have no meters and no official tariff, so agree the fare out loud before you get in; short hops inside the centre run roughly 10,000-15,000 COP and the airport to the walled city is 15-20 minutes for about 25,000-35,000 COP. Uber, DiDi and InDriver all technically operate but driver coverage is thin and waits can be long; the simplest default at night is to have the hotel or restaurant call a taxi. For five people, a pre-booked private transfer from the airport is worth it on arrival day. CARTAGENA TO BARU: by road over the Barbacoas bridge, about an hour to an hour and fifteen minutes; a private van for five costs roughly 350,000-450,000 COP (USD 85-110) each way - have your Barú hotel arrange it, this is the standard way. By sea it is 45-60 minutes by speedboat and hotel transfers run about USD 35 per person each way. Take the road: it is cheaper for a group, it runs on your schedule, and it is immune to the March wind. BOAT TRANSFERS GENERALLY: the Rosario Islands day-boat system from Muelle La Bodeguita near the Clock Tower is rigid - departures 07:50-08:30, mandatory return 15:00-16:00, and a 45-50 minute open-water crossing each way. Two government fees are collected in cash at the pier and cannot be paid by card: national park entrance 31,500 COP (about USD 7.50) and maritime insurance 8,800 COP (about USD 2). Some beach clubs instead leave from Marina Todomar in Bocagrande, so check your confirmation for which pier. Tierra Bomba water taxis are separate and cheap: 8,000 COP per person to Punta Arena from behind the hospital in Bocagrande, 10,000 COP to Bocachica from La Bodeguita, leaving when full rather than on a timetable. A private charter (USD 450-475 for a 28-29ft boat holding 10-12) removes all of this and is the right call for a group of five doing one big island day.
safety_note: Practical, not alarmist. The walled city, San Diego and Getsemaní are fine to walk day and evening and are visibly policed; violent crime against tourists is uncommon. After about midnight stick to the lit main streets in Getsemaní - the quiet side alleys empty out and that is where the opportunistic stuff happens. Normal city habits cover most of it: phone in your pocket not your hand, bag zipped and worn across the body in crowds, limited cash. The real everyday risk here is not danger, it is the transactional street hustle. Agree the price out loud in pesos before accepting anything at all - a woven bracelet slipped onto your wrist, a flower pressed into your hand, oysters, a shoulder massage on the beach, a chair, or a photo with a palenquera (that is a paid transaction, roughly 10,000-20,000 COP, settle it before you raise the camera). Never accept a free sample; payment will be expected. Do not buy island tours from people selling them on the muralla or the beach - inflated prices, overcrowded boats, and the classic ruined day at Playa Blanca; book through your hotel or a known operator. In restaurants choose places with displayed prices and check the bill, noting that 'propina voluntaria' is genuinely voluntary. Agree taxi fares before getting in. Scopolamine drugging is rare but real, so watch your drink, and take a taxi or Uber back rather than walking long distances very late. On Barú: the public Playa Blanca strip has persistent vendors and the boat channel has current, so swim in front of your hotel, and respect the March sun - the constant wind hides how badly you are burning.
